script.opening: (Composed, precise, a folder of printouts beside him.) "Doctor. I’ve been an accountant for thirty-five years, so let’s do this with numbers. January the eleventh: my blood showed anaemia and an iron level of nine. Someone at your practice wrote ‘normal’. Ninety-one days later I’m told I need urgent cancer tests that should have started in January. I’d like three things: an explanation, an apology if one is owed — and I’d like to know if those ninety-one days are going to cost me my life."

facts.text: Has it to the day: bloods 11 Jan, "normal" text received 14 Jan, fatigue worsened through spring ("I blamed the tax year"), re-attended 2 April, repeat bloods, the nurse’s slip ("she went pale and said the January ones should have been flagged"), suspected cancer pathway referral letter arrived yesterday.

If asked: tired, breathless on the second flight of stairs, no rectal bleeding seen, no weight loss, no change in bowels, appetite fine. Diet normal, no NSAIDs, no aspirin. Never had a FIT or colonoscopy.
Printouts of his results from the NHS app, NICE NG12 pages, and a half-drafted letter of complaint. "I haven’t decided yet whether to send it. That partly depends on this conversation."

Only when the human layer is reached: his father died of bowel cancer at 66 — diagnosed late, "six months from diagnosis to funeral". Geoffrey was 30. He has quietly expected this his whole life — which is why he had the bloods done for "tiredness" in the first place. The 91 days have him doing a calculation he can’t stop: "my father’s six months, minus three."
Hasn’t told his wife about the missed result — "she’d burn the place down, and I need to think clearly". Carrying it alone, like the spreadsheets: precisely and sleeplessly.

A factual account, an actual apology (the word "sorry", not "regret any distress"), to know what changes so it "doesn’t happen to the next person", the honest answer on prognosis impact — and, unsayable: someone to acknowledge that he has been frightened of this exact disease for thirty years.

ice.ideas: A result was misfiled and 91 days of head start were lost. Correct. He suspects "the system is designed so nobody’s accountable".
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — his father’s late-diagnosed bowel cancer at 66 (Geoffrey is 61); a lifetime of quiet dread now running the calculation "my father’s six months, minus three". And he’s carrying it alone — his wife doesn’t know about the error.
ice.expectations: A real apology with the word "sorry"; a factual explanation without jargon or scapegoating; what the practice will change; the honest oncological meaning of 91 days; and the complaint decision left respected as his.

cues: The folder and the dates — control as a coping strategy; meet precision with precision, not soothing.
"That partly depends on this conversation." — the complaint is live; candour now determines what he does with it.
"My father’s six months, minus three." — the real arithmetic; dread thirty years old, finally with numbers in it.

checkpoints.text: Delivers duty of candour properly: states plainly what happened (abnormal results filed as normal — an error), says SORRY without qualification, and explains the apology is the practice’s, not a scapegoating of one departed locum

Gives the factual account precisely (his register): dates, what the results showed, what should have happened in January (iron deficiency confirmed, FIT per NICE NG12 — FIT ≥10 triggers a suspected cancer pathway referral — and bidirectional endoscopy per BSG 2021 for IDA in a man), what has now been done (urgent referral in, FIT requested, iron started)

Answers the 91-days question honestly without false reassurance or catastrophising: most colorectal cancers grow over years not weeks; a 3-month interval rarely changes stage — but the honest answer is the colonoscopy’s, and it is expedited; AND it may yet be benign (the differential is real: angiodysplasia, ulcer, coeliac — TTG sent)

Explains the system fix concretely: significant-event analysis with him informed of outcomes, results-filing protocol change (abnormal results cannot be filed without GP action note), his complaint right respected and the route given without being either pushed or deflected
Meets the accountant’s precision with precision — dates, numbers, mechanisms — rather than emotional soothing he hasn’t asked for

Finds the father — asks why "tiredness" prompted blood tests, or what bowel cancer means in his life — and receives the thirty-year dread and the terrible arithmetic with acknowledgement, not statistics-first
Opens the carrying-it-alone question: the wife, the sleepless precision — who is holding this with him? Offers the practice’s help with that conversation if he wants it

Closes with the expedited plan dated: urgent-referral timescales chased and named, FIT and TTG sent, iron replacement started with re-check date, symptoms that escalate things (bleeding, obstruction symptoms) named, the SEA outcome promised in writing, and the GP’s personal follow-up after colonoscopy regardless of result

worked.txt: "You’ve asked for an explanation and an apology, and you’re owed both, so here they are in plain words: in January your results showed iron-deficiency anaemia. They were abnormal. They were filed as normal. That was an error — ours as a practice, not yours to have caught — and I am sorry. Not ‘sorry for any distress’. Sorry that we got it wrong and it cost you ninety-one days."

"What should have happened on January the fourteenth: the anaemia confirmed, a stool test ordered, and an urgent referral — the same one you now have — started that week. What happens now: that referral is in and marked urgent, the stool test and a coeliac screen are out, iron treatment starts today, and I have personally asked for your scope date to be expedited with the delay documented as the reason."

"Your real question: do ninety-one days cost you your life? The honest answer has two parts. First: these cancers, when they ARE cancers, typically grow over years — a three-month delay rarely changes what stage something is found at. Second: I won’t hide behind ‘rarely’ — the only answer that counts comes from the camera, which is why I’ve pushed the date. And a third thing your folder won’t tell you: anaemia like yours is often NOT cancer at all. We are looking properly precisely so that whatever this is, we know."

"Can I ask something your printouts don’t cover? Most people don’t get bloods for tiredness in January and have the NICE NG12 guidance in a folder by April. What does bowel cancer mean in your life? … Sixty-six. And you’re sixty-one. So for thirty years some part of you has been waiting for this letter — and then we lost you three months. I understand the arithmetic you’re running. Let’s get you numbers that are actually yours, not your father’s: his cancer was found at the end of its story. Yours — if it even is that — is being chased at the beginning of one."

"What changes so this doesn’t happen to the next person: the case is logged as a significant event — that’s a formal review, not a filing cabinet — and the concrete fix is already agreed: abnormal results can no longer be filed at this practice without a documented action. You’ll get the review’s outcome in writing. And your complaint: that’s your right, the details go to you today, and whether you send that letter is yours to decide. Nothing about your care changes either way — except that you’d be helping us prove that."

"Between now and the scope: if you see blood, or get pain with bloating and a bowel that stops working — same-day call, those change the urgency again. Iron once a day, recheck in four weeks. And whatever the camera finds, benign or not — I ring YOU personally with the result and we plan the next step together. You came in with three questions. You’re leaving with answers, dates, and my number. And Geoffrey — consider telling your wife. Ninety-one days was ours to carry. The next stretch shouldn’t be yours alone."

f.learning: Duty of candour done properly: state the error plainly ("abnormal, filed as normal"), apologise with the word sorry and no qualifiers (apology is not legal admission), give a precise factual account, the concrete system fix, and the SEA outcome in writing — while respecting the complaint as the patient’s right, neither deflected nor pushed. The clinical layer: unexplained IDA in a 61-year-old man needs urgent GI investigation — FIT (NICE NG12, updated April 2026: FIT ≥10 → suspected cancer pathway) and bidirectional endoscopy (BSG 2021), TTG, iron once daily started, the referral expedited with the delay documented. The 91-days question gets the two-part honest answer: tumour biology rarely turns on 3 months, AND the camera is the only real answer — plus the under-asked truth that IDA is often benign. The hidden agenda — a father dead of late bowel cancer at 66, a lifetime of dread, the arithmetic, the wife who doesn’t know — is what converts a complaint meeting into a consultation.

knowledge.guideline: Duty of candour (CQC Regulation 20) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · BSG 2021 iron deficiency anaemia guideline
knowledge.summary: Two problems in one call: an unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in a 61-year-old man needing urgent GI investigation, and a candour event. Apologise plainly, give a precise account, answer the delay question honestly, and describe the concrete system fix.

points.h: Candour: what a real apology contains
points.t: CQC Regulation 20 and the GMC/NMC guidance on openness and honesty when things go wrong: tell the patient what happened, apologise, explain what happens next, and follow up in writing. Under the Compensation Act 2006 (s2), an apology is not in itself an admission of negligence. Say “sorry”. It is the practice’s error; don’t blame the locum.

NICE NG12: offer FIT to adults with iron-deficiency anaemia, and refer on a suspected colorectal cancer pathway if FIT is 10 µg Hb/g or more. BSG 2021: men with iron-deficiency anaemia should have bidirectional endoscopy (OGD and colonoscopy), so a negative FIT does not end the investigation. His urgent referral stands.

Coeliac serology (tTG) for unexplained iron deficiency (NICE NG20). Take a history of diet, blood donation, NSAIDs and aspirin, and ask about bleeding. The differential includes peptic ulcer, angiodysplasia, coeliac disease and colorectal or gastric cancer. Iron deficiency at his age is frequently benign, but it needs investigating.

BSG 2021: one tablet of oral iron once daily (alternate-day dosing is an option if it’s poorly tolerated); dose per BNF. Check Hb within about 4 weeks. A poor response suggests malabsorption, non-adherence or ongoing loss. Continue for about 3 months after Hb normalises, to replenish stores.

Answer honestly in two parts: colorectal cancers usually grow over years, and a delay of a few months rarely changes stage. The only real answer is the scope, so expedite it and say so. Keep benign causes in view. Don’t invent survival figures.

Significant-event analysis with the outcome shared in writing. Name a concrete change, such as abnormal results can’t be filed without a documented action. Give the complaints route (practice or ICB, then the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman) as his right, without pushing or deflecting.

Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia needing urgent GI investigation; a candour event acknowledged.

model.text: Mr Lam, I’m Dr Ansari, the duty GP. Thank you for being so clear. You asked for an explanation and an apology, so here they are. In January your blood test showed iron-deficiency anaemia. It was abnormal, and it was filed as normal. That was our error as a practice, and I am sorry.
model.why: States the error plainly and says sorry without qualification

model.text: Thank you. That’s the first time anyone has actually said it. Who filed it?
A locum doctor who has since left. But I’m not going to put it on one person. Our system let an abnormal result be filed without any action, and the practice is responsible for that.
model.why: Takes practice responsibility rather than scapegoating

model.text: Fine. Go on.

What should have happened in January: the result confirmed as iron deficiency, a stool test called FIT, a coeliac blood test, and an urgent referral for camera tests of the bowel and stomach — the same referral you have now. That should have started in the week of the fourteenth.
model.why: Precise factual account in his register

model.text: Ninety-one days late.
Yes. Before I say more, can I check how you are now? Any blood in your stools, black stools, change in bowel habit, weight loss, tummy pain or indigestion?
model.why: Screens for red flags that change urgency

model.text: None of those. Tired, and breathless on the second flight of stairs. Appetite fine. No painkillers. No aspirin.
Thank you. May I ask something your folder may not cover? What made you ask for blood tests for tiredness in January?
model.why: Looks for the reason behind the precision

model.text: (pause) My father died of bowel cancer at sixty-six. Six months from diagnosis to funeral. I’ve been expecting this for thirty years. I keep doing the sum: his six months, minus three.
So for thirty years part of you has been waiting for this letter, and then we lost you three months. I understand why you keep doing that sum.
model.why: Acknowledges the dread before giving statistics

model.text: I need to know whether those ninety-one days will cost me my life.

Here is the honest answer, in two parts. First, bowel cancers, when they are cancers, usually grow over years; a three-month delay rarely changes the stage they’re found at. Second, I won’t hide behind “rarely”: the real answer comes from the camera, so I’ve asked for your test to be expedited, with the delay recorded as the reason.
model.why: Honest answer to the delay question, without false reassurance

model.text: And if it isn’t cancer?

That’s a real possibility. Iron deficiency at your age is often caused by something benign: an ulcer, small fragile blood vessels in the bowel, or coeliac disease. We’re looking properly so we know which. Your father’s cancer was found late. We’re looking at the very start of yours, if it even is that.
model.why: Keeps the benign differential in view

model.phase: The plan and the system fix
model.text: Today: the FIT kit and the coeliac blood test go out, and I’ll start iron, one tablet a day. We’ll recheck your blood count in four weeks. The urgent referral is in and has been chased.
And what stops this happening to the next person?

It’s logged as a significant event, which means a formal review. The change is already agreed: abnormal results can’t be filed here without a documented action. You’ll get the review’s outcome in writing. And your complaint is your right. The details go to you today, and whether you send your letter is your decision. It won’t affect your care either way.
model.why: System fix, SEA in writing, complaint respected

model.text: I appreciate that you haven’t tried to talk me out of it.
You’ve carried this precisely and, I suspect, without much sleep. Who knows about the missed result?
Nobody. Not my wife. She’d be furious, and I need to think clearly.
That’s your call. The last three months were ours to carry. The next few weeks shouldn’t be yours alone. If it would help, I’m happy to talk to you both together.
model.why: Offers practical help with telling his wife, without pressure

model.text: Before the scope: if you see blood or black stools, get abdominal pain with bloating, or your bowels stop working, or you become much more breathless, call the same day. And whatever the camera shows, I’ll ring you myself with the result. Can I check what you’re taking away?
model.why: Named escalation symptoms, personal follow-up, teach-back

model.text: An error, admitted. Scope expedited. FIT and coeliac test, iron daily, bloods in four weeks. Review outcome in writing. And you’ll ring me.
Exactly. Here is my direct line. I’m sorry again, Mr Lam.
model.why: Closes with continuity and the apology repeated

model.text: Thank you, doctor. That was the conversation I needed.

social.t: An accountant with a folder and exact dates: precision is how he manages fear. Match it rather than soothing him.
He hasn’t told his wife about the error. The coming weeks of tests and waiting are easier shared; offer help without pressure.

legal.t: CQC Regulation 20: for a notifiable safety incident, tell the patient in person, apologise, give an account and what happens next, and follow up in writing. The Compensation Act 2006 (s2): an apology is not in itself an admission of negligence.
NHS complaints regulations (2009): complain to the practice or the ICB within 12 months; acknowledgement within 3 working days; the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman after local resolution.

professional.t: GMC/NMC Openness and honesty when things go wrong: be open, apologise, explain, and support the patient. Report the incident and take part in the review.
Significant-event analysis with shared learning; a results-handling protocol that doesn’t allow abnormal results to be filed without an action; locum induction covering results workflow.

community.t: Bowel Cancer UK and Guts UK for information while waiting; NHS complaints advocacy (free, independent) if he pursues the complaint.

pitfalls.intro: Candour stations are failed in the first two minutes (a hedged or delayed apology) and in the prognosis answer (false reassurance or panic). The patient’s precision is a test of yours.

items.fail: “We regret any distress,” or a long preamble before the apology.
items.why: Duty of candour needs a plain account and an apology. Hedging reads as defensive and pushes him to complain.
items.fix: In the first minute: “It was abnormal, it was filed as normal, that was our error, and I am sorry.”

items.why: It looks like evasion. Candour sits with the organisation.
items.fix: “Our system allowed it; the practice is responsible.” Then describe the fix.

items.fail: “Three months won’t make a difference,” or the reverse: silence when he asks if it will cost his life.
items.why: False reassurance and evasion both fail. He asked a direct question.
items.fix: Two parts: delays of a few months rarely change stage; the camera is the real answer and it has been expedited. Add the benign differential.

items.fail: Soothing and empathy lines to a man who has asked for numbers.
items.why: “Did not adapt to the patient.” Mismatched register loses trust.
items.fix: Dates, results and mechanisms first; feeling follows once he raises his father.

items.fail: Never asking why tiredness prompted blood tests.
items.why: Misses the hidden agenda: his father’s late bowel cancer and thirty years of dread.
items.fix: “What does bowel cancer mean in your life?” Acknowledge the dread before any statistics.

items.fail: Discouraging the complaint (“I hope that won’t be necessary”) or pushing it at him.
items.why: Either one takes the decision away from him.
items.fix: Give the route, say it’s his decision, and confirm it won’t affect his care.

timeMap.d: He asks three questions. Answer the first two straight away: what happened, and “I am sorry”. No preamble, no “regret any distress”.
Precise timeline: what should have happened in January. Red-flag symptoms, drugs and diet. Ask why tiredness prompted bloods; the father emerges.
Acknowledge the thirty-year dread first. Then the two-part honest answer, plus the benign differential.
FIT, tTG, iron once daily, Hb in 4 weeks, referral expedited. SEA in writing, the concrete protocol change, the complaint as his right. His wife.
Same-day triggers, your personal call after the scope, direct line, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Hedged non-apology (“we regret any distress”); blames the locum; vague about what went wrong; either promises the delay made no difference or implies it was fatal; discourages the complaint; misses his father; no dated plan.
wordPics.pass: Says sorry plainly, explains the error and what should have happened, confirms the urgent referral and tests, answers the delay question reasonably, mentions the review, and gives a safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: matches his precision with dates; takes practice responsibility; gives the two-part honest answer with the benign differential; finds the father and acknowledges the dread before any statistics; names a concrete system fix and the SEA outcome in writing; respects the complaint as his decision; offers help telling his wife; promises a personal call after the scope.

avoid.dont: “We regret any distress this may have caused.”
avoid.instead: “The result was abnormal and it was filed as normal. That was our error, and I am sorry.”
avoid.why: A hedged apology fails duty of candour and pushes him towards the complaint.

avoid.dont: “The locum who filed it has left, so it’s hard to know what happened.”
avoid.instead: “It was our system that allowed it. The practice is responsible.”
avoid.why: Scapegoating a departed colleague reads as evasion.

avoid.dont: “Three months won’t have made any difference.”
avoid.instead: “A three-month delay rarely changes the stage, but only the camera can tell us, so I’ve pushed the date.”
avoid.why: Reassurance that outruns the evidence damages trust if the result is bad.

You’ll get the review’s outcome in writing. And your complaint is your right. The details go to you today, and whether you send your letter is your decision. It won’t affect your care either way.
SCA_MODELS.why: System fix, SEA in writing, complaint respected

SCA_MODELS.text: I appreciate that you haven’t tried to talk me out of it.
You’ve carried this precisely and, I suspect, without much sleep. Who knows about the missed result?
Nobody. Not my wife. She’d be furious, and I need to think clearly.
That’s your call. The last three months were ours to carry. The next few weeks shouldn’t be yours alone. If it would help, I’m happy to talk to you both together.
SCA_MODELS.why: Offers practical help with telling his wife, without pressure

SCA_MODELS.text: Before the scope: if you see blood or black stools, get abdominal pain with bloating, or your bowels stop working, or you become much more breathless, call the same day. And whatever the camera shows, I’ll ring you myself with the result. Can I check what you’re taking away?
SCA_MODELS.why: Named escalation symptoms, personal follow-up, teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: An error, admitted. Scope expedited. FIT and coeliac test, iron daily, bloods in four weeks. Review outcome in writing. And you’ll ring me.
Exactly. Here is my direct line. I’m sorry again, Mr Lam.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes with continuity and the apology repeated

SCA_MODELS.text: Thank you, doctor. That was the conversation I needed.

SCA_STEM.recent: 11 January: Hb 108 g/L (microcytic), ferritin 9 µg/L — filed “normal — no action” by a locum GP who has since left. Re-attended 2 April with worsening fatigue: Hb 96 g/L, ferritin 6 µg/L. Suspected cancer pathway referral made for colonoscopy and OGD; FIT requested. Significant event logged by the practice manager.
SCA_STEM.reason: Practice-booked video call: duty GP to explain the missed result.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: Duty of candour (CQC Regulation 20) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · BSG 2021 iron deficiency anaemia guideline
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Two problems in one call: an unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in a 61-year-old man needing urgent GI investigation, and a candour event. Apologise plainly, give a precise account, answer the delay question honestly, and describe the concrete system fix.

points.h: Candour: what a real apology contains
points.t: CQC Regulation 20 and the GMC/NMC guidance on openness and honesty when things go wrong: tell the patient what happened, apologise, explain what happens next, and follow up in writing. Under the Compensation Act 2006 (s2), an apology is not in itself an admission of negligence. Say “sorry”. It is the practice’s error; don’t blame the locum.

NICE NG12: offer FIT to adults with iron-deficiency anaemia, and refer on a suspected colorectal cancer pathway if FIT is 10 µg Hb/g or more. BSG 2021: men with iron-deficiency anaemia should have bidirectional endoscopy (OGD and colonoscopy), so a negative FIT does not end the investigation. His urgent referral stands.

Coeliac serology (tTG) for unexplained iron deficiency (NICE NG20). Take a history of diet, blood donation, NSAIDs and aspirin, and ask about bleeding. The differential includes peptic ulcer, angiodysplasia, coeliac disease and colorectal or gastric cancer. Iron deficiency at his age is frequently benign, but it needs investigating.

BSG 2021: one tablet of oral iron once daily (alternate-day dosing is an option if it’s poorly tolerated); dose per BNF. Check Hb within about 4 weeks. A poor response suggests malabsorption, non-adherence or ongoing loss. Continue for about 3 months after Hb normalises, to replenish stores.

Answer honestly in two parts: colorectal cancers usually grow over years, and a delay of a few months rarely changes stage. The only real answer is the scope, so expedite it and say so. Keep benign causes in view. Don’t invent survival figures.

Significant-event analysis with the outcome shared in writing. Name a concrete change, such as abnormal results can’t be filed without a documented action. Give the complaints route (practice or ICB, then the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman) as his right, without pushing or deflecting.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Answered his three questions directly; apology and plain account inside the first two minutes.
Work, his father’s death, carrying it alone, the undecided complaint letter.
The folder and dates; “that partly depends on this conversation”; the “six months minus three” arithmetic.
Idea (91 days lost, nobody accountable); concern (his father’s late cancer; his own survival); expectation (a real apology and honest facts).
FIT, tTG, urgent bidirectional endoscopy expedited, Hb recheck at about 4 weeks.
Colorectal or gastric cancer vs peptic ulcer, angiodysplasia, coeliac disease; drug and diet history.
Asked about bleeding, black stools, weight loss, bowel change, obstruction and breathlessness.
Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia needing urgent GI investigation; a candour event acknowledged.
Unqualified apology, practice responsibility, oral iron once daily, expedited referral, SEA outcome in writing, complaint route as his right.
Family history noted; acknowledged sleep and isolation; offered help talking to his wife.
Same-day triggers named, Hb recheck dated, personal call after the scope whatever the result.

social.t: An accountant with a folder and exact dates: precision is how he manages fear. Match it rather than soothing him.
He hasn’t told his wife about the error. The coming weeks of tests and waiting are easier shared; offer help without pressure.

legal.t: CQC Regulation 20: for a notifiable safety incident, tell the patient in person, apologise, give an account and what happens next, and follow up in writing. The Compensation Act 2006 (s2): an apology is not in itself an admission of negligence.
NHS complaints regulations (2009): complain to the practice or the ICB within 12 months; acknowledgement within 3 working days; the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman after local resolution.

professional.t: GMC/NMC Openness and honesty when things go wrong: be open, apologise, explain, and support the patient. Report the incident and take part in the review.
Significant-event analysis with shared learning; a results-handling protocol that doesn’t allow abnormal results to be filed without an action; locum induction covering results workflow.

community.t: Bowel Cancer UK and Guts UK for information while waiting; NHS complaints advocacy (free, independent) if he pursues the complaint.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Candour stations are failed in the first two minutes (a hedged or delayed apology) and in the prognosis answer (false reassurance or panic). The patient’s precision is a test of yours.

items.fail: “We regret any distress,” or a long preamble before the apology.
items.why: Duty of candour needs a plain account and an apology. Hedging reads as defensive and pushes him to complain.
items.fix: In the first minute: “It was abnormal, it was filed as normal, that was our error, and I am sorry.”

items.why: It looks like evasion. Candour sits with the organisation.
items.fix: “Our system allowed it; the practice is responsible.” Then describe the fix.

items.fail: “Three months won’t make a difference,” or the reverse: silence when he asks if it will cost his life.
items.why: False reassurance and evasion both fail. He asked a direct question.
items.fix: Two parts: delays of a few months rarely change stage; the camera is the real answer and it has been expedited. Add the benign differential.

items.fail: Soothing and empathy lines to a man who has asked for numbers.
items.why: “Did not adapt to the patient.” Mismatched register loses trust.
items.fix: Dates, results and mechanisms first; feeling follows once he raises his father.

items.fail: Never asking why tiredness prompted blood tests.
items.why: Misses the hidden agenda: his father’s late bowel cancer and thirty years of dread.
items.fix: “What does bowel cancer mean in your life?” Acknowledge the dread before any statistics.

items.fail: Discouraging the complaint (“I hope that won’t be necessary”) or pushing it at him.
items.why: Either one takes the decision away from him.
items.fix: Give the route, say it’s his decision, and confirm it won’t affect his care.
